concept.name: Sunk-cost fallacy
concept.definition: The tendency to continue an endeavor because of previously invested, unrecoverable resources - money, time, or effort - even when prospective costs exceed prospective benefits. Rational choice requires ignoring sunk costs (the bygones principle); Arkes and Blumer (1985) documented the systematic violation.
concept.intuition: 'I have already lost so much on this trade that I cannot sell now' - but the money is gone regardless of what you do next.
concept.mechanics: Past investment is treated as justification for future commitment, driven by loss framing (selling realizes a loss), personal responsibility for the initial decision, and the desire not to appear wasteful. In trading it appears as adding to losers or holding positions past their invalidation point.
concept.failure_modes: Not all persistence is fallacious: abandoning a position too early can be its own error, and outsiders may lack the decision-maker's information. The label is warranted only when forward-looking expected value no longer justifies continued exposure.
concept.misconceptions: Cutting a position because it is a sunk cost is rational only when the forward outlook no longer justifies holding; the fallacy is letting the past loss, rather than the future expectation, drive the decision. Sunk costs are also not the same as fixed costs.
concept.example: A trader doubles down on a losing position to get back to breakeven, increasing exposure to a trade whose original thesis has already failed.
